objectives: Pick the right binary search template for a new problem.
Count pairs in a sorted array with one binary search per element.
Combine search on the answer with a greedy check.

sections.heading: Intuition: three templates cover almost everything
paragraphs: This week used three binary searches. Exact search asks "is it here?" and stops when found. Lower bound asks "where does the first value ≥ x start?" First-true asks "what is the smallest k where the check says yes?", even when k isn't an index into anything.
The lower bound and first-true are really the same loop: lo = mid + 1 on no, hi = mid on yes. Most new problems come down to choosing the yes/no question and the starting range.
bullets: Exact match in sorted data: day 8.
First position with value ≥ x, or counting values below x: day 10.
Smallest amount that is enough: day 13.

callout.text: Before coding, write down three things: the yes/no question, why every no comes before every yes, and a starting range that surely contains the answer.

sections.heading: Baseline: check every pair
paragraphs: Counting pairs i < j with values[i] + values[j] ≤ T by trying every pair takes O(n²). For 100,000 values that's about five billion checks.

sections.heading: Worked example: count pairs with a small enough sum
paragraphs: Sort the values. For a fixed i, partners j that work are all at the start of the part after i, because the values only grow. So binary search for the first j where values[i] + values[j] > T. Every index between i + 1 and that j is a partner.

For [1, 2, 4, 5, 7] and T = 6: from 1, the first partner that's too big is 7 at index 4, giving 3 pairs. From 2, it's 5 at index 3, giving 1 pair. From 4 on, there are none. Total 4. Counting only j > i means each pair is counted once.

diagram.description: Sorted values 1, 2, 4, 5, 7. For the 1, the partners 2, 4, 5 form one block; 7 is too big.

sections.heading: Your turn: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
paragraphs: Today's first medium. Each flower blooms on a given day. A bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers. Return the minimum number of days to make m bouquets, or -1 if impossible.

callout.text: What becomes easier as the number of days grows? Write a check for one day count first.

sections.navLabel: Your turn: Maximum Distance Between a Pair of Values
sections.heading: Your turn: Maximum Distance Between a Pair of Values
paragraphs: Today's second medium. Two arrays are both non-increasing. A pair (i, j) is valid if i ≤ j and nums1[i] ≤ nums2[j]; its distance is j - i. Return the largest distance.

callout.text: Fix an i. Which j values are valid, and do they form one block? Then consider whether you even need binary search.
callout.title: Where to start

sections.heading: Complexity and cautions
paragraphs: Pair counting with binary search: O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log n) for the searches. Next week you'll count the same pairs with two pointers in O(n) after sorting.
Products and sums of two large values can overflow 32-bit integers; use 64-bit math.

sections.heading: Before you finish
paragraphs: Try to answer each question before opening it.

checks.prompt: Why does counting only j > i avoid double counting?
checks.answer: Each unordered pair has exactly one smaller index, so it's counted once, from there.

checks.prompt: Why do the good partners of i form one block?
checks.answer: The array is sorted, so values[i] + values[j] only grows as j grows. Once a sum is too big, every later one is too.

checks.prompt: Which template fits "the fewest days until something is possible"?
checks.answer: First-true search on the answer, with a check for a given number of days.
